title: Indian Startup Miraqules Wins SLINGSHOT 2026 Grand Prize in Singapore
excerpt: The Bengaluru medtech's SeeStop powder, designed to stop severe bleeding in about 12 seconds, took the S$100,000 Startup SG Grant and the top Health and Biomedical honours at SWITCH.
body:
• Miraqules MedSolutions of Bengaluru won the Grand Prize at SLINGSHOT 2026, Enterprise Singapore's global deep-tech pitching competition, held during SWITCH on October 28.
  • The prize package is a S$100,000 Startup SG Grant, a sponsored trip to Singapore and an 18-month EntrePass, according to CNA.
  • Its product, SeeStop, is a powder made of electrospun nanofibres designed to stop severe bleeding in about 12 seconds without pressure or tourniquets, based on the company's pre-clinical results.
  • Miraqules also won its Health and Biomedical domain category; the product is not yet commercially approved, and trials and regulatory clearance are still ahead.

SINGAPORE — An Indian medtech startup whose powder is designed to halt severe bleeding in seconds has won the Grand Prize at SLINGSHOT 2026, the global deep-tech pitching competition run by Enterprise Singapore during the Singapore Week of Innovation and Technology (SWITCH).

Miraqules MedSolutions, based in Bengaluru, took the top honour on October 28 along with first place in the Health and Biomedical domain, according to CNA. The Grand Prize carries a S$100,000 Startup SG Grant, a sponsored trip to Singapore and an 18-month EntrePass work visa. SLINGSHOT's 2026 edition offered more than S$2.2 million in grant prizes across its finalists, drawn from a global field of startups.

A powder built to buy minutes

Miraqules' product, SeeStop, is a sterile powder made from electrospun polymer nanofibres. Sprinkled on a wound, the nanofibres absorb blood and form a gel-like seal over the injury. The company says the dressing stopped bleeding in about 12 seconds in pre-clinical testing, works without applied pressure, tourniquets or sutures, and is designed to stay in place during transport before being washed off with water or saline at a hospital.

The company positions the product for the settings where uncontrolled bleeding kills fastest: road accidents, battlefields, disaster zones and rural areas far from a trauma centre. Miraqules is led by chief executive Mubeen Khan and chief technology officer Mudassir Ansari, and has previously been recognised by India's Department of Biotechnology ecosystem, including a place among the top startups at Global Bio-India.

Why Singapore, and what comes next

SLINGSHOT is Enterprise Singapore's flagship competition for deep-tech startups, run through the SWITCH festival, and it is designed to plug winning companies into Singapore's research, hospital and investor networks. For an Indian medtech at Miraqules' stage, that matters as much as the grant: the company still has to complete clinical validation and win regulatory approvals before SeeStop can be sold, and Singapore offers a fast route to hospital pilots and Southeast Asian markets.

The win also continues a pattern Indian founders know well. India's medtech sector has produced globally competitive devices before, but trauma care — where most preventable deaths occur before a patient reaches surgery — has drawn less venture money than diagnostics or hospital software. A hemostat that works in 12 seconds without training-intensive equipment is aimed squarely at that gap, and at the ambulances, police first responders and military medics who reach patients first.

The honest caveat

SeeStop's headline numbers come from the company's own pre-clinical work, not from published human trials, and no regulator has yet cleared the product for sale. Plenty of promising wound-care technologies have stalled between animal studies and approval. What SLINGSHOT's judges have certified is the strength of the science and the size of the problem — Miraqules itself describes its technology and history on its company site. The clinical proof is the test still to come.

For the Indian diaspora's large community of clinician-founders and health-tech investors in Singapore and the United States, the result is a marker: an Indian deep-tech medical device, built in Bengaluru, has beaten a global field on a Singapore stage. Whether it reaches ambulances will be decided by trials, not pitch decks.
